items.title: 4.7.2 Maximum amount of product and amount of any unreacted excess reagent

blocks.title: Excess reagent
blocks.text: The reactants present in larger amounts than the stoichiometry of the reaction needs, which remain unreacted at the end of the reaction, are the excess reagents (excess or non-limiting reactants).

Consider 2H2(g) + O2(g) gives 2H2O(l). When 2 moles of hydrogen (4 g) react with 2 moles of oxygen (64 g), only 2 moles (36 g) of water form, because 2 moles of hydrogen need only 1 mole (32 g) of oxygen; hydrogen is the limiting reactant. When 1 mole of O2 and 1 mole of H2 are mixed, all the hydrogen reacts and oxygen is left over, because 1 mole of H2 needs only half a mole of O2; the remaining half mole is excess.
Sample Problem 4.19: 30 g of CH4 with 50 g of O2

Methane burns as CH4 + 2O2 gives CO2 + 2H2O. Step 1, write the balanced equation. Step 2, moles of each reactant: CH4 = 30 / 16 = 1.875 mol; O2 = 50 / 32 = 1.563 mol. Step 3, product from each: 1 mol CH4 gives 1 mol CO2, so 1.875 mol CO2; 2 mol O2 give 1 mol CO2, so 1.563 x 0.5 = 0.7815 mol CO2. Oxygen gives less, so O2 is the limiting reactant. Step 4, mass of product: 0.7815 x 44 = 34.39 g of CO2. Step 5, the limiting reactant fixes how much excess reactant is used: 2 mol O2 react with 1 mol CH4, so 1.563 mol O2 use 1.563 x 1/2 = 0.7815 mol CH4. Step 6, excess left = taken - used = 1.875 - 0.7815 = 1.0935 mol CH4, which is 1.0935 x 16.0 = 17.5 g of methane unreacted.
